source_read: PDF (version of record), Psychiatry Research 365 (2026) 117430, pp. 1-13 (all pages read in a pdftotext extraction; Tables 1-3 checked on pages rendered at 150 dpi; Figs. 1-6 read on the rendered pages, Figs. 2-6 at 300 dpi; supplementary material not among the files). Only the parts of the claim from this source were checked; the Pearson (2013) parts are another reader's.

claims.overstatement: One phrase is not supported: 'a step not described as planned' for removing Larimer et al. (2007). The Methods describe influence diagnostics (studentized residuals, Cook's distance) 'with sensitivity analyses conducted by excluding influential studies' (p. 3, 2.7 Data synthesis); only the subgroup analyses are called prespecified, and the PROSPERO protocol was not read. Suggested wording: 'after removing the trial with the most weight (Larimer et al., 2007, about 47% of the weight, g -0.03), flagged by influence diagnostics although the trials did not differ (I2 0%)'. Smaller points: 'all outcomes were self-reported' goes slightly beyond the paper, which names 'reliance on self-reported outcomes' as a limitation (p. 11) without saying all were; 'a meta-analysis of 15 randomized trials' - 15 trials were included in the review, but only 11 contribute to any pooled estimate (Braitman and Henson 2016, Dvorak 2015, Edwards 2020 and LaBrie 2015 appear in none of Figs. 3-6, without a stated reason), so the pooled figures rest on 9, 6, 7 and 6 of 11 trials. Everything else from this source, including the pooled estimates, subgroup figures, risk of bias, attrition and mediation counts, is supported and not overstated; the claim's 'very small' and 'possibly' match the intervals.
claims.note: Checked on the rendered pages (Figs. 2-6 at 300 dpi). All pooled numbers match text and forest plots. Re-pooling the plotted study estimates (DerSimonian-Laird, editors' check; the paper used Jamovi MAJOR, presumably REML) reproduces problems -0.068 (-0.137 to 0.000) and without Larimer -0.102 (-0.195 to -0.008), strategy use without O'Donnell 0.234 (0.065 to 0.403), and the subgroups: over 3 months quantity -0.12 (Braitman 2018, Kenney, Larimer, Leeman, Martens) and frequency -0.13 (Braitman 2018, Larimer, Leeman, Martens); the adjunct frequency estimate -0.13 reproduces only from the four adjunct trials (Andersson, Larimer, Leeman; Neighbors has no frequency data), not adjunct plus booster (-0.11), although the Methods define the subgroups as core/primary against adjunct/booster (p. 3); so the claim's 'three of the four multi-component trials also gave personalized normative feedback' (Andersson, Larimer, Neighbors; Table 2) fits the subgroup as analysed. Larimer et al. (2007), mailed personalized feedback with normative content, is in both 'larger effect' subgroups and is the most precise trial in each analysis. Risk of bias: Fig. 2 shows 1 low (Martens 2013, which found no effect on drinking or harms), 10 some concerns, 4 high (Arazan, Braitman and Henson, Braitman and Lau-Barraco, Dvorak); the text says three high (p. 5): the claim's '14 of the 15' holds either way and the magnitude's '10 some concerns, 4 high (Fig. 2)' matches the figure. Mediation: text 3 of 6 significant (p. 6), Table 3 and the Discussion name 4 (Dvorak, Kenney, LaBrie, Larimer; p. 8), as the claim says. 'One 45-person pilot': O'Donnell 2019, 45 randomized and 38 analysed (Table 1), g 2.89 (1.97 to 3.80). Overlap with the Pearson part of the claim: Sugarman and Carey (2009) and Larimer et al. (2007) are both among the 15 trials (Table 1), as the claim says. Not checked here: the Pearson (2013) parts of the claim, and the examples 'eating' and 'alternating drinks', which are not in this paper (its examples are drink limits, pacing and a designated driver or safe transport).

anchors.extracted: PBS interventions: people explicitly taught, prompted or reinforced to use intentional behaviours before, during or after drinking to reduce intake or harm; three domains, limiting or stopping (e.g. drink limits), manner of drinking (e.g. pacing), harm reduction (e.g. designated driver); PBS had to be a primary or clearly identifiable delivered component, alone or within multi-component interventions; comparators no intervention, waitlist, standard care, education or other behavioural interventions; adults 18 or over.

anchors.locator: 2.7 Data synthesis, 2nd to 4th paragraphs; 2.5 Risk of bias assessment
anchors.extracted: Random-effects meta-analyses (Jamovi, MAJOR) of Hedges' g from post-intervention data at the longest follow-up, one effect per study per model; prespecified subgroups by follow-up (3 months or less against more) and role (core/primary against adjunct/booster); influence diagnostics with sensitivity analyses excluding influential studies; no risk-of-bias sensitivity analysis because only one trial was low risk.

anchors.locator: 3.1 Study selection and overview, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Fig. 1 (p. 4); Table 1 (p. 6)
anchors.extracted: 15 RCTs published 2007 to 2023, mostly in universities: 13 in the USA (86.7%), 1 Sweden, 1 Australia; samples 45 to 9,277; mostly undergraduates aged 18 to 24, one study up to 35 (O'Donnell 2019). Searches to December 2025; Fig. 1 gives 514 records (the five database counts add to 564), 456 screened, 59 + 12 reports assessed, 20 not retrieved.

anchors.locator: 3.2 Characteristics of interventions, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Table 2 (p. 7)
anchors.extracted: Most interventions combined PBS domains (11 all three; 4 selective avoidance and alternatives); no study evaluated a single PBS domain in isolation, so domain subgroups were impossible; roles core 4, primary 4, booster 3, adjunct 4 (46.7% secondary); mostly single-session or brief and digital, 4 with face-to-face contact. Table 2: the adjunct trials are Andersson (PNF + PBS), Larimer (PNF + PBS), Leeman (US-THRIVE + PBS) and Neighbors (PNF + PBS + BAC feedback).

9 trials: g -0.05 (95% CI -0.13 to 0.02), p = 0.162, I2 22.0%, prediction interval -0.18 to 0.07; no influential outliers or publication bias. Trial estimates range from -0.54 (Leeman 2016) to +0.30 (Sugarman 2009).
6 trials: g -0.09 (-0.17 to -0.02), p = 0.014, I2 11.85%, prediction interval -0.19 to 0.001. Only Larimer 2007 (-0.16, -0.26 to -0.06) is significant alone.

7 trials: g -0.07 (-0.14 to 0.0007), p = 0.052, I2 0%; influence diagnostics flagged Larimer et al. (2007) (largest square, g -0.03, -0.13 to 0.07); without it g -0.10 (-0.19 to -0.01), p = 0.034, heterogeneity unchanged.

anchors.locator: 3.4.4 Protective behavioral strategy use; Fig. 6 (p. 10); Table 1 (p. 6)
anchors.extracted: 6 trials: g 0.58 (-0.21 to 1.37), p = 0.152, I2 97.8%, prediction interval -1.47 to 2.63; O'Donnell 2019 (pilot, 45 randomized, 38 analysed; g 2.89, 1.97 to 3.80) an outlier; without it g 0.23 (0.07 to 0.40), p = 0.005, I2 49.9%.

anchors.locator: 3.4.5 and 3.4.6 Subgroup analyses; 4. Discussion, p. 10, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Over 3 months: quantity g -0.12 (p = 0.004), frequency -0.13 (p = 0.003); nothing significant at 3 months or less. Adjunct: quantity -0.10 (p = 0.040), frequency -0.13 (p < 0.001); core or primary: no significant effect on quantity, problems -0.11 (p = 0.091), strategy use 0.91 (p = 0.128). Only g and p in the text (intervals in supplements, not seen); no test of the difference between subgroups is reported; the authors call these exploratory (p. 10).

RoB 2. Text: overall risk 'low to moderate'; one trial low in all domains, three high, the rest some concerns. Fig. 2 overall column: 1 low (Martens 2013), 10 some concerns, 4 high (Arazan 2023, Braitman and Henson 2016, Braitman and Lau-Barraco 2018, Dvorak 2015).
Attrition 0% to 95%, highest in large digital trials; Arazan 2023 88-95% (9,277 randomized, 658 analysed), Braitman and Lau-Barraco 2018 70-79%, Braitman and Henson 2016 40-67%.

anchors.locator: 3.3 Integrated summary of effects, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Table 3 (p. 8); 4. Discussion, 2nd paragraph (p. 8)
anchors.extracted: Six trials ran mediation analyses; text: three found indirect effects through PBS; Table 3 and the Discussion name four (Dvorak 2015, Kenney 2014, LaBrie 2015, Larimer 2007), with Martens 2013 and Neighbors 2009 not significant. Several trials raised PBS use without reducing drinking or harms (Arazan, Martens, O'Donnell, Sugarman and Carey); Braitman 2022 and Leeman 2016 reduced drinking without PBS change.

Limits named by the authors: mostly young US university students; few studies per analysis; few formal mediation tests and no temporal order; reliance on self-reported outcomes, heterogeneous definitions, inconsistent fidelity reporting, interventions combining PBS domains; high-risk trials kept and no risk-of-bias sensitivity analysis.
Trials in the pooled analyses: 11 of 15. Braitman and Henson 2016, Dvorak 2015, Edwards 2020 and LaBrie 2015 appear in no forest plot; no reason is given.

Sugarman and Carey (2009; 177 students, 2 weeks) and Larimer et al. (2007; 1,488 students, 12 months) are among the 15 trials; Table 3: Sugarman, PBS use increased without less drinking; Larimer, drinking reduced with effects mediated by PBS (though its PBS change is marked 'not assessed').

The abstract leads with the post-outlier strategy-use estimate (g 0.23) and calls the problems result 'significant in sensitivity analysis'; it concludes that PBS interventions 'produce modest, context-dependent effects'; the Conclusion calls them a promising but context-dependent approach.

key_findings.correction: Editors' sums recomputed from Table 1: 15,714 randomized, 6,587 analysed.

Could add: Larimer et al. (2007) carries about 47% of the inverse-variance weight in this pool (editors' calculation from the Fig. 5 intervals); re-pooling the plotted estimates reproduces -0.07 and -0.10 without it.
Locator detail: the 1st paragraph of 3.3 starts at the foot of p. 5 and its counts are on p. 6.

reporting_issues.note: Fig. 2 overall column at 300 dpi: high for Arazan 2023, Braitman and Henson 2016, Braitman and Lau-Barraco 2018, Dvorak 2015; low for Martens 2013 only.
Fig. 2 D3 (missing outcome data) for Arazan is green (low); Table 1 gives 9,277 / 658 and 88-95% attrition for a posttest-only design.
Also LaBrie 2015 (251 / 251, attrition NR) and Sugarman and Carey 2009 (177 / 177, 0%).

Text p. 6 (three) against Table 3 and Discussion p. 8 (four); Table 2 'None' against Table 3 'Moderation (ns)' for Braitman 2022; Larimer 'Not assessed' with mediation via increased PBS use (Table 3).
Table 3 'Yes' for PBS change: Arazan, Dvorak, Edwards, Kenney, LaBrie, Martens, Neighbors, O'Donnell, Sugarman (9); Table 2: Andersson and Arazan list two domains.

Six trials, not five, had three or more arms (Table 1, p. 6): Andersson 2015 (5 arms), Leeman 2016 (4), Braitman and Lau-Barraco 2018, Braitman 2022, Martens 2013 and Sugarman and Carey 2009 (3 each). The rest of the issue stands; re-pooling the plotted estimates suggests the adjunct subgroup is the four adjunct trials only (frequency -0.13 reproduces from Andersson, Larimer and Leeman; adding the boosters gives -0.11), so the three booster trials appear to have been left out of the role comparison or analysed separately (editors' reconstruction; supplements not read).

risk_of_bias.note: AMSTAR 2, low confidence (provisional): item 4 'no' (English, peer-reviewed limits not justified; no registries or grey literature) is the one critical flaw; item 7 no information without Appendix 2; items 11 and 13 close calls as the card says. Item 9: the lenient D3 judgment for Arazan is noted; it does not change the rating.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor, borderline moderate: the abstract gives only the post-removal strategy-use estimate (the prespecified pooled 0.58, p = 0.152, is absent), calls problems significant in sensitivity analysis, and states greater effects for two subgroups without a between-subgroup test; all three are labelled, and the alcohol results are reported fairly. The results text also calls overall risk of bias low to moderate (p. 5) when 14 of 15 trials had some concerns or high risk.

missed: Only 11 of the 15 trials enter any pooled estimate: Braitman and Henson 2016, Dvorak 2015, Edwards 2020 and LaBrie 2015 appear in none of Figs. 3-6, and no reason is given. They include two of the four trials credited with mediation through PBS (Dvorak, LaBrie) and one of the three with reduced harms (Edwards). Claims should say 'pooled from 9, 6, 7 and 6 of 11 trials' rather than imply a 15-trial meta-analysis.

Subgroup membership (editors' re-pooling of the plotted estimates, approximate): over 3 months = Braitman 2018, Kenney, Larimer, Leeman, Martens for quantity (-0.12) and Braitman 2018, Larimer, Leeman, Martens for frequency (-0.13); adjunct = Andersson, Larimer, Leeman, Neighbors. Larimer et al. (2007; mailed feedback with normative content, 12 months, the most precise trial) is in both 'larger effect' subgroups, so the two findings largely overlap.

The Methods describe influence diagnostics 'with sensitivity analyses conducted by excluding influential studies' (p. 3, 2.7). The card's 'not described as prespecified' is accurate (the word is used only for the subgroups), but the step was described as part of the analysis plan; the claim's 'a step not described as planned' goes beyond the paper.
The Discussion (p. 8, 2nd paragraph) cites Braitman 2022 as reducing alcohol outcomes without PBS change, but Table 3 marks Braitman 2022 'Alcohol reduction: No' (drinking declined in all arms).

Table 3's trial-level verdicts do not always match the pooled inputs: Kenney 2014 harm reduction 'Yes' against g -0.03 (-0.30 to 0.23) in Fig. 5; Neighbors 2009 PBS change 'Yes' against g 0.19 (-0.05 to 0.42) in Fig. 6; presumably other time points or measures, not explained.

The only low-risk trial (Martens 2013) found no effect on quantity (-0.12, -0.37 to 0.13), frequency (0.06) or problems (-0.15, -0.40 to 0.11) despite raising PBS use (0.49, 0.23 to 0.74) (Figs. 3-6).

The card's 'self-reported drinking and problems in every trial' (exposure) goes slightly beyond the paper, which lists reliance on self-reported outcomes as a limitation (p. 11) without saying every trial; Table 3 lists BAC outcomes (Andersson, Braitman and Henson, Neighbors) whose method is not described.
